Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. In the context of the just released May lay-off figures showing that almost 4,000 Canadians were laid off in May in addition to those who were laid off in April, and also in the context of the rather strange speech given by the Minister of Finance to the CMA last evening in which the minister indicated that businessmen in Canada on many occasions are given a ten-point tax advantage compared with their counterparts in the United States, would the minister indicate to the House why we are having these continued lay-offs in Canada, and has he any particular suggestion as to how the situation can be corrected?

Mr. Speaker, there are always some problems in certain areas of the economy. However, I think the hon. member could have mentioned that there was an increase of 12.6 per cent in car and truck sales in Canada from May to May. I said in my speech in Toronto that, contrary to the rumours spread around by the hon. member, when we do a thorough study of the comparison between the Canadian tax system and the American tax system, we find that our tax system for corporations is very competitive with the American system: it is even better.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Minister of Finance. In the May budget of four years ago, Mr. Turner, referring to the manufacturers' and processors' incentives that the government of the day had given to the various businessmen in Canada, said that he anticipated a great expansion in industry. Four years later, in April of this year, we find that we have 18,000 fewer people working in manufacturing in Canada.
Would the minister indicate if he feels that the incentives given the manufacturers and processors at that time have not worked; or, if he feels that they have worked, would he indicate why there appears to be a lack of confidence to which he referred last evening when he was speaking to the CMA?

Would the minister indicate whether he is entirely happy with his budgetary stance at the present time and does not contemplate any changes, notwithstanding the fact that not only were there 4,000 persons laid off last month but 3,000 of them were laid off in Ontario alone?

We had a budget recently, and I just gave an example of provisions in the budget that are working very well. For example, the fact that we have cut the sales tax on cars has produced dramatic results, as well as the fact that we had an increase of 12.6 per cent from May to May.

speakeroldname: Mr. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
speechtext: My question is directed to the Prime Minister. Last week the Prime Minister attended the NATO meetings in Washington and it was expected that he would be discussing with the other leaders at those meetings the questions of the GATT negotiations, particularly in view of the fact that the Americans have taken the position that there must be substantial agreement by July 15, that their authority to negotiate will run out at the end of the year and in view of our serious economic problems. Did the Prime Minister have any bilateral discussions on that subject last week and, if so, with what effect and with whom?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, there was no attempt, and no intention on the part of any of the participants, to discuss the matters in the context of the NATO summit held in Washington last week. I did have some bilateral meetings or discussions with other leaders, some of whom will be attending the summit in Bonn in the middle of July, and I did express views there about the importance of not only looking at short-term improvements but at medium and long-term improvements in our economies, including trading patterns.

In view of the fact that the government's figures show a loss of 80,000 manufacturing jobs between the end of 1974 and the end of 1977, and in view of the difficulties that we are having in the television industry, where the sale of Canadian TV sets has fallen almost 30 per cent and where
4,500	jobs have been lost in the last several years in that industry alone, as well as serious declines in furniture and other industries and, as the Science Council points out, deindustrialization is posing a real threat to Canada, can the Prime Minister tell the House what is his strategy at the GATT negotiations to protect Canada from further injury to the manufacturing industry and a further loss of jobs, particularly

June 6, 1978
Oral Questions
in view of the July 15 deadline? What is our strategy to avoid harm to ourselves and to our productive sector?

As the Minister of Finance just replied in answer to a previous question, within a free economy there are moving patterns of development. In the case of Canada, we like to see jobs created in all sectors, but the trend nowadays in most industrialized, advanced societies is to create more jobs in the service sector: this is happening in Canada. In so far as the rate of creation of jobs is concerned, we have told the hon. member before that between last year and the same time this year some 330,000 jobs were created in Canada. That is a faster job-creation rate than exists in any other industrialized society.

The 4,500 people who have lost their jobs in the television parts manufacturing industry would be interested to hear the Prime Minister's figure of the number of jobs being created. They have lost 4,500 jobs. Could the Prime Minister tell us, in relation to that particular industry, why the government has not taken action such as the successful action the United States has taken to reduce its imports from Japan in April by 60 per cent and the over-all importation of television sets by 30 per cent by using voluntary import quotas? That is the step the United States has taken. It is one of the great manufacturing countries of the world. Why has the Prime Minister's government not taken similar steps? When will he direct his minister to take some steps to save this industry?

Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member had been following the debates on international trade, he would have seen that the government took various steps to get agreement from other countries trading with Canada on their export quotas to Canada. As a general direction in Canada, which is a trading nation to a much larger degree than the United States in the sense that a larger percentage of our wealth comes from trading than in the United States, it is important to maintain a general principle of free trade in every direction.
Rather than asking the economies of the world to go toward greater protectionism by quotas or by tariffs, we are going in the other direction. We have confidence that the Canadian economy, given a fair chance of competition with other nations, will meet that competition and will excel in it.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. In view of the admitted weak position the government has taken in pursuing a clear policy on economic boycotts, which was evidenced in the Prime Minister's speech to the United Jewish Appeal, is it the Prime Minister's position that the only leadership he can bring to this serious problem is to focus the public spotlight on any company which is refused government trading support? In other words, are we to have legislation by press release now, and how does this affect a company which does not apply to the government for support through EDC for financing or insurance? speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is expressing his own view when he says the policy is weak. If he looks around the world, I believe he will find that Canada and the United States are the only two countries which have policies in this regard, and those policies are not considered weak by people who want to trade in the Middle East.
If the hon. member looks at the report tabled by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, he will Find that a great many companies were forced to come around and respect the government's policies and not respect the boycott clauses. middle East, and those companies which do not have assistance from the Government of Canada and its various agencies have a very difficult time trading there. That is why we believe our policy is effective, and the facts demonstrate that it is.

Get the facts straight.

Just because you misstate the facts.

I wish they would look at the report tabled by the minister: they would see what effect the policy has had and they would realize that the companies in Canada that want to trade with the Middle East do need the Canadian government's assistance, and we say they will not have it unless they do not adhere to boycott policies. Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State. It concerns the fact that Canada Council grants have been given to such organizations as Pulp Press, of Vancouver, publishers of a book called "Minimanual for the Urban Guerrilla", and the tabloid "Strike", of Toronto which, incidentally was banned at the Bologna art fair in Italy two days ago. Will the minister tell the House what reasons justify the granting of public funds to organizations such as these which advocate terrorism, kidnapping, kneecapping, legshooting and murder?

Mr. Speaker, 1 think it is only fair to point out that when the grant to which the hon. member refers was issued, the publication "Strike" had not appeared and the organization concerned appeared to be devoting itself entirely to matters of cultural concern. As a result-
What kind of culture?

As a result of the change in the nature of the publication to which the hon. member has referred and as a result of representations which have been made in this House and outside the House, I have written to the Canada Council to draw to their attention the concerns of members and the concerns of the public, and I am waiting for further information.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary for the Secretary of State arises from remarks he is reported to have made a few days ago to the Senate and Commons committee concerning public access to government information, and specifically to reports stating that he said he was in favour of freer information, and I quote his words, "rather than on the side of holding back".
How does the minister reconcile such a statement with his utterance, widely quoted in the press, in a speech to the Toronto Liberal forum on May 10, 1978, to the effect that as long as he is Secretary of State, members of parliament will not be allowed information on the reasons for the giving or otherwise of Canada Council grants, a thing which, if done, would probably prevent such things as the incidence of "Strike", and so on?

Mr. Speaker, the point that I was making in the speech in Toronto was that there is a distinction to be made between over-all policy considerations and the day to day administration of independent agencies such as Canada Council, particularly in relation to the granting process. Parliament has not given me the power to interfere in the day to day grant process. It is not a power which I wish to have. There is a considerable degree of difference between ranging through the files of the Canada Council in order to influence the way in which those decisions are taken, and access to information which is necessary for the conduct of public business.

Mr. Speaker, the minister says that he does not have the power to interfere with the Canada Council, yet a moment ago he said that he wrote to the Canada Council with regard to a specific grant. I ask him, is he prepared to conduct a full investigation of the Canada Council to determine how many other such instances there are like the Pulp Press and the tabloid "Strike" and a number of others that anyone in this House could mention, an investigation long overdue and long needed; and will he not allow input from members of parliament and others across the country as to how these decision-making processes are arrived at?

MR. McRAE-PROCEEDINGS OF STANDING COMMITTEE ON NATIONAL RESOURCES AND PUBLIC WORKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege as a member of the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works. On December 1, 1977, that committee was given a reference from this House to report on the management of nuclear waste, the Hare report.
Since that time the committee has had 19 meetings. There have been many challenges to the report. A particularly strong challenge came from the president of the Geological Association of Canada, which we take very seriously since that particular challenge deals with the geological work that has to be done in order to bury the waste.
The committee made an interim report on March 15 because it felt there might have been an election, in which case the committee wanted the work to go on, if the session ended, into a new parliament. It is my understanding that in their report the committee indicated that, in the interim, the government should consider doing research on the matter. Two more meetings are scheduled for next week. The committee's work has been revived.
Yesterday the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) tabled in this House a document entitled "Canada-Ontario Radioactive Waste Management Program" which, in my opinion, completely upstages the work that the committee was doing. That document states that Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and Ontario Hydro have signed agreements to do work, research and otherwise, on the waste totalling between $90 million and $150 million.
Ontario Hydro has gone ahead in spite of the fact there is a Porter royal commission in Ontario looking at this very matter. AECL has gone ahead in spite of the fact the standing committee of this House is also looking into this matter.
As a member of that standing committee, I believe I have a question of privilege in the sense that I attended most of the 19 meetings where this was being very seriously considered. In fact we are still looking at it. The committee work is not finished, yet for all practical purposes decisions have been made. The contracts have been signed. Also, we must remember the approximately 150 people who wrote briefs, appeared before the committee, and so on. In my opinion, all that work is for naught.
If I have a question of privilege, I would be willing to move, seconded by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid), that the action of AECL be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.

That, in relation to Bill C-56, an act to amend the statute law relating to income tax and to authorize payments related to provincial sales tax reductions, one sitting day shall be allotted to the further consideration of the second reading stage of the said bill; and
That at fifteen minutes before the expiry of the time provided for government business in such sitting, any proceeding before the House shall be interrupted, if required, for the purpose of this order and, in turn, every question then necessary in order to dispose of the second reading stage of the bill shall be put forthwith and successively, without further debate or amendment.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING
speechtext: The House has heard the terms of the motion, it being moved in accordance with the provisions of Standing Order 75C. Debate pursuant to this motion now begins and, under the rule, has a duration of two hours.

subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the evening of April 10, I made a budget speech in the House. Then there was a six-day debate on the budget. After several votes, the budget was passed by the House of Commons. I then introduced the bill now under consideration, Mr. Speaker, and we have now entered the tenth day of debate at the second reading stage. Under the terms of my motion, we will have had 11 days to debate the bill on second reading. There will then be the committee of the whole which will study each one of the 60 clauses in this bill. Then, we will have third reading. Here we are in June and we have already spent 16 days on this bill.
Moreover, we have other bills to introduce in the House of Commons, including Bill C-48 resulting from the budget and concerning customs and excise, a bill I will introduce tomorrow on orders of the day and through which we want to simplify the operations of small businesses by reducing their capital gains tax and also by allowing income tax deductions for people who invest in small businesses, and there is also a bill which the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) wants to introduce in the House and other legislation. Because of statements by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) that he would do a filibuster, the opposition has refused to co-operate with the government. I am making use of the Standing Orders to allot some of the time of the House to
80045-19y2

June 6, 1978
S.O.	75C
dispose of this bill. Moreover, this debate has gone on ad nauseam in the House. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and myself have replied to dozens of questions concerning this issue and there remains no problem of principle to settle.
First of all, the opposition asked us to send a cheque of $226 million to the Quebec government. Since then, the Quebec government has abandoned its friends in the opposition and no longer asks that the $226 million be sent directly. Then, it was suggested last week that a tax collection agreement could be entered into with the Quebec government but they never intended to give anything in exchange to the federal government. Considering that since 1954, the Quebec government, bent on upholding the principles of provincial autonomy, has always assumed its own responsibilities with regard to income tax collection, and considering that after reading the morning newspapers, it already becomes obvious that it no longer wants us to proceed with tax collection on its behalf, we will resolve the only remaining problem when we come to Clause 30 of the bill, that is devising a way to compensate Quebec citizens because we have been unable to come to an agreement with their government.
We did propose a formula which appears in Clause 30 of the bill. Instead of using the 1977 taxpayer rolls as a basis for proceeding with a tax reduction, I suggested at that time that income tax be lowered so that a $100 fiscal abatement could be granted to the taxpayers for the year 1978. Now, we will decide on that, following whatever direction the debate might take, when we get to clause 30 but it seems absolutely useless to pursue the matter now.

I would like to make a few points regarding the budget. Very few people have spoken about the measures we have put forward which must be made law. It was published today that, because of the present economic circumstances and the fact that we reduced by 3 per cent the sales tax on automobiles and trucks, there has been an increase of 12.6 per cent in the sales of automobiles and trucks this past year.
Many people have said over and over again that the way I have chosen to cut taxes across the board for all items is wrong. This morning I saw a report to the effect that retail sales in stores increased by 4.9 per cent in April. What is very amazing is that in B.C. the increase was 16 per cent. It was 4.6 in Ontario; and in Quebec, where the Quebec government chose to do things its own way, there was a decrease of .8 per cent in sales in the month of April. The truth will come out when all the figures are available.
The measure we have proposed is a first in the history of Canada. This is the first time a minister of finance has gone across the land and talked to all ministers of finance to try to develop a consensus.

subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING

Everyone agreed that on the afternoon of budget day I would call them, and they would say yes or no to

my proposition. Every minister of finance complied with that gentleman's agreement, everyone but one. After that, Mr. Speaker, I had to proceed.

I think that under the circumstances enough time was lost in the House by the people who do not care at all about what we are trying to do, to develop, for the first time in this land, economic policies in conjunction with the provinces.

subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING
speechtext: The opposition was very quick to jump in bed with the people who have only one goal in mind, namely, to destroy the Canadian Confederation.

subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING
speechtext: I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that there is no problem with the constitution. I recognized on the first day of the consultation that the sales tax was a provincial matter, because I consulted the provinces. I made a proposal to which eight of the provinces agreed and with which one has disagreed. They can do whatever they want in their jurisdictions, and in fact they have done what they wanted to do, and I have not intervened. But I have to do what I want to do in my own jurisdiction. What I did on the night of the budget was to reduce the income tax of all the citizens in the other provinces. I do not want to penalize the people of Quebec because Mr. Parizeau saw fit not to join the national scheme, because it was an occasion for all of us ministers of finance in this land to develop a new mechanism for participation by the provinces in the economic policies of this nation.

subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING
speechtext: Of course, Mr. Parizeau wanted to maintain the status quo to try to prove a point, but I am not for the status quo. I tried, in the spirit of the meeting of first ministers in February, to develop co-operative policies among the ministers of finance, and today I would like to thank all the ministers of finance in the land who have agreed with me in the spirit of collaboration and co-operation following the first ministers' conference.

subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING
speechtext:
But of course, as was the case at the first ministers' conference, after three days of debate the premier of Quebec saw fit to grandstand and to quit just to try to make his case for nothing. Why was he there if he did not agree to anything? The same thing happened with my proposal. I acted
June 6, 1978

in good faith and in the best spirit of collaboration in trying to evolve new economic policies for this land, but of course Quebec, in a self-serving attitude, tried to throw a wrench into my scheme.
I am very sorry that members on the other side do not think at all about what it was all about. They are just preoccupied with trying to score some political points, but the people of Canada will judge them very severely for just playing politics.

subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have just had another of those pitiable, shameful performances by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien).

subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING
speechtext:
When the Minister of Finance gets into trouble, he wraps himself in the Canadian flag and says that everybody who is criticizing him is criticizing the country. "What is wrong with that?", asks one deposed minister in the back row. What is wrong with that is that it is fundamentally dishonest and it badly serves the cause of federalism, when a minister of the Crown is wrong and when he is accused of being wrong, not to answer the accusations, not to deal with the evidence, but instead to dismiss all of his critics, ranging from Claude Ryan to the Toronto Globe and Mail, if you can think of a compass that large, as separatists.
What is of interest here is that the Minister of Finance by his actions, by his unparalleled incompetence as Minister of Finance, has set back severely the very process he celebrates of co-operation with the provinces. He admits his own incompetence. He stands up in the House of Commons and tells us once more that he went into an agreement which required the agreement of the provinces, knowing he did not have the agreement of the one province which he knew was going to stand up and hit him if he tried to bring in a measure to which they had not agreed. That is naivete, it is simple incompetence, and it is a serious disservice to this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING
speechtext: We will have an opportunity to discuss this matter at some length later on, unless the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his henchmen intend to introduce closure clause by clause, because what is of interest here is that this is not even normal closure. Normal closure applies when the government thinks it is right, when the opposition thinks it is wrong, and when the government uses its power to force its way through. In this case the government does not even pretend that it is right-the government knows that it is wrong. Yesterday the Minister of Finance in the House admitted that he knows he is wrong. He admitted that he is going to back away from the proposal to which we take exception.

subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING
speechtext: That is flexibility.

subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING
speechtext:
He is certainly flexible. We oppose this measure for one major reason. I do appreciate hearing the Minister of
S.O.	75C
Finance confirm that he knows he is wrong, confirm that he is going to back down on the proposal which has held up debate in the House.
We are opposing this measure for one major reason, that is, that it invades the jurisdiction of the provinces. The minister has said he will change that, and he just repeated it. But he will not tell us how he wants to use the most extreme power of parliament to force us to accept something the key contents of which we do not know. Is provincial jurisdiction going to be respected here? Is the government abandoning its proposal to pay a direct cheque to everyone in Quebec and not pay a direct cheque to the citizens in other provinces? Is the economic stimulus to the province of Quebec to be delayed for a year? The government will not say, yet, sir, those are the questions that the whole dispute is about. If the government answers those questions in a way that respects provincial rights, and in a way that treats Quebec as it treats the other provinces, then there would be no need for closure. But this government would rather abuse power than use simple common sense.

subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING
speechtext:
This bill embarrasses the government. They made a serious mistake in acting as though they had agreement, when they did not have it. They made another mistake in the Prime Minister's stubborn refusal to admit he was wrong. Now they have to back down. They are discussing new arrangements with Quebec. They should have done that weeks ago and not delayed the business of parliament debating a bill which they knew they would have to change. Now that they are forced to back down, what they should do is to withdraw the bill for two or three days and to amend it. That is what they would do if they respected parliament. But they do not, so we have closure.

And why resort to closure? It is not because the debate has dragged on; on the main motion, there have been 10 speakers; four Liberals, four Progressive Conservatives and two NDP members; on the amendment, we heard 25 speakers, eight of whom were Liberals. The minister wants to close the debate before some other Liberals are compelled to speak. Most of all, he does not want parliament to hear the views of the hon. members for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Joyal), Matane (Mr. De Bane) and Compton (Mr. Tessier) about the infringement of provincial rights.

The use of closure is just one more indication of the incompetence of the Minister of Finance. He talked about his record in bills. He has introduced six bills in this session and he has had to invoke closure on two of them. He promised an employment tax credit, then he took three months to write the bill and another three months to get the forms out. That proposal was supposed to generate 50,000 new jobs-it generated only 1,900. His inability to see the trap that Quebec set for him created this problem, which has seriously harmed the cause of federalism. It is this government, by its foolishness

June 6, 1978
S.O.	75C
and stubbornness, that has set back the cause of federalism and given momentum to the Parti Quebecois.

subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING
speechtext:
Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, why not withdraw the bill temporarily, allow the minister to make whatever changes he can and let parliament deal with other matters in the meantime, and then bring forward an amended bill that parliament, the government and the provinces can accept? This government is too stubborn to admit to being mistaken. Closure is at times invoked on a matter of principle; but in this case its use is dictated by the stubbornness of the government.

A government is judged not only by the things it does but by the way it uses its power. This is a government which condones secret trials in Canada. I see the Prime Minister is smiling. This is because he was the author of the action. This is a government which imprisons innocent citizens without charge. It is a government which now uses a form of closure to force through parliament a measure which the government knows is wrong and knows it is going to change. That is an abuse of the rules of parliament. It is an abuse of the role of the provinces. It is an abuse of the rights of the citizens of Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to oppose the motion introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). In so doing, I want to make it clear that there are times in debates in the House of Commons when a responsible government will introduce such a motion. It is in the rule book. It is there for use by the government to make a decision as to when a debate is over. If the opposition is still going on with what it regards as a relevant debate, and if the government can make a good case to end it, the government can decide to exercise that responsibility and bring the debate to a conclusion. But if there ever was a circumstance where closure was completely inappropriate, surely this is it.
The original proposal made by the government in principle was accepted by all of the other provinces. It was amended in detail to accord with the basic principle that it was satisfactory for the federal government. The province of Quebec came along and made a proposal which was fully in accordance with the principle of the bill and was fully in accordance with its constitutional responsibilities, but it consisted of a process which made the federal minister feel he was outmanoeuvred politically, and the federal government said no. Because the federal government wants a partisan battle is no reason to play games with the federal system in Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING
speechtext:
That is exactly what is involved in this matter. A few minutes ago the minister indicated in the debate

that the Quebec government made its proposal after the fact. With all due respecl I say to the minister that it was not up to the government of the province of Quebec, or the governments of any other provinces, to reach an agreement according to the time table imposed by the federal government. In an area of jurisdictional authority which is within provincial domain, surely it is a right of the province of Quebec, or of any other province, to negotiate a deal which meets its legitimate constitutional interests.

subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING
speechtext:
I say that with all the emphasis I can. The province of Quebec was constitutionally right in its judgment. Also it was pragmatically right in terms of the details of its proposal and the ideas put forward. If any of the other provinces had wanted a delay, they would have been entitled to the same kind of delay. In a matter as fundamental to the federal system as this, I cannot understand how the Minister of Finance could have brought in a budget offering this type of deal to the provinces without all provinces being in agreement in advance, particularly considering the situation in the province of Quebec at this time.
At an earlier phase in this debate I gave credit to the minister. I repeat that credit now. I meant it earlier and I mean it now. I give him credit for involving the provinces. In a federal state when it is necessary to take stimulative measures involving fiscal policy, the time to start using this system imaginatively is long overdue. Indeed from time to time the federal government brings in a measure which has direct impact in an area of provincial jurisdiction, such as in this case. It is important for the minister to consult with the provinces and arrive at an agreement so that we can manage our federal state much more efficiently and competently from an economic point of view. To the extent that we have received some innovation from the Minister of Finance in these circumstances, I repeat that he deserves credit.
At the same time I cannot overemphasize my own view. Certainly it is one which is shared unanimously on this side of the House, as well as by many people outside the House who are not opposition party members. My view is that the Minister of Finance made a colossal political blunder and a colossal misjudgment of political reality in this country when he brought in this measure without the agreement of the province of Quebec. He should have recognized that this area is particularly sensitive to the province of Quebec, not simply with the present government but indeed with preceding governments such as Union Nationale governments and Liberal governments of that province. This is demonstrated by the fact that he sees himself in opposition not only to the existing provincial government of the province of Quebec but to all opposition parties as well. It was a colossal error in judgment on the part of the Minister of Finance when he brought in this measure.
The question we are dealing with is whether closure is legitimate now. Is it? I cannot think of a worse time to invoke closure. There is no pressing priority. The federal government indicated that an agreement has not been reached and that it is
June 6, 1978

still discussing proposals with the province of Quebec. It is asking us to buy a pig in a poke, which is an old metaphor that is entirely appropriate, especially when one considers clause 30. We do not know what the amendment will be. Why could the government not accept the proposal I made in all sincerity two weeks ago when I moved a 30-day hoist, rather than the traditional six-month one? I moved that 30-day hoist to provide us with a cooling off period, perhaps to arrive at some agreement on this central matter.
Why could the government not accept the argument which has been made by all parties in the House? That argument was reasserted today by the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). All we have to do is put this bill aside. We do not need to pass it in its present form. In fact, we should not pass it. The argument indicating that we in the opposition are holding up parliament is absurd. The people who are holding up progress in parliament now are the Government of Canada, not the opposition parties.

subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTMENT OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-56 ON SECOND READING
speechtext:
All the government has to do is withdraw this bill.
I do not doubt that the Minister of Finance is sincere when he indicates that he is talking about it and that they are going to bring in an amendment. If he has some hope that it may yet be agreeable to the province of Quebec, why does he not use his common sense and put this bill aside? Then we could move on and discuss other measures, instead of the government invoking closure and using its majority to pass a bill which will be amended down the road. In fact, we do not even know what the substance of the amendment will be. I do not think a good argument could be made for invoking closure at this point. As I have said, we should simply stop debate and go on with other measures.
In conclusion, 1 want to say that my party still believes the legitimate constitutional position argued by the province of Quebec in this case is an acceptable one. The minister made special deals with British Columbia, Saskatchewan, and all the Atlantic provinces. He was prepared to be flexible with those regions. Why in God's name is he not prepared to be flexible with the government of Quebec?
When I say that we should give the government of Quebec every cent it is entitled to and not one penny more or less, just as every other province has received, I do not speak alone. The Saskatchewan minister of finance is prepared totally for the Minister of Finance to write out the cheque and send it to the government of the province of Quebec. The government of Saskatchewan realizes constitutionally that it negotiated one package which was acceptable to it. Also that province realizes that the package acceptable to Quebec is different in detail but similar in principle. The same constitutional point holds: Quebec should receive its fair share. I say to the minister, get busy, write the cheque, drop this bill for now, and let us get on with the other work.

Mr. Speaker, I never expected that this action would be proposed to put an end to the debate on this very serious question. A short while ago, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) said in his remarks that this debate had lasted long enough since his budget was presented on April 10. I admit that the proceedings on this matter have been going on for some time, but we must admit that it is a very important issue and that it should not be dealt with lightly, if we want to avoid making a tremendous mistake that would further prejudice the harmony in our country.
In my opinion, the proposal put forward by the Minister of Finance, as I indicated earlier, flies in the face of our constitution. The fact that we most urgently need to draw up a new constitution does not mean that the Minister of Finance may well violate the present one. He must respect it pending a new one that will determine more precisely the rights and responsibilities of the provinces as well as the rights and responsibilities of the central government. Mr. Speaker, in my view, Bill C-56 is some kind of an all-encompassing bill. It is somewhat the government's habit, when it wants to get the House to pass an unacceptable measure to integrate it into a bill including other acceptable measures in order to embarrass the hon. members. I find these practices deplorable, and I cannot condone them. Again, I ask the Minister of Finance to amend clause 30 of the bill in order to respect provincial jurisdiction. The minister has repeated many times that through this measure he wants to increase consumer purchasing power.
I am very happy about that, everyone is, but he used means that violate the constitution; that is why the Quebec government and all parties represented in the National Assembly oppose this bill, as I do; as a member of the Canadian parliament coming from Quebec, I must oppose it-which I am doing in a positive way-I am convinced the Minister of Finance stepped out of line. If he only took one step back, he would fall in the right place. The whole country would be pleased and would say "There goes a great man, the Minister of Finance". He recognized that he took a step in the wrong direction but he stepped back and starting from there he introduced another measure. I suggested and discussed with him last week the possibility of decreasing or cancelling completely the tax at the manufacturers' level which falls within federal jurisdiction. When I put the question here in the House, even the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said it was an excellent idea. It might even be the ideal formula. However, we are afraid that wholesale dealers will take advantage of the situation to increase their profits.
Mr. Speaker, I say to the Minister of Finance that he is quite well supported by economists and competent officials who are surely able to prevent those who would try to take advantage of the situation from increasing their profits at the consumers' expense. I promised that I would bring him this

June 6, 1978
S.O.	75C
week a bill which was prepared by a member of the U.S. House of Representatives a few years ago, a bill which explains fully how to implement the formula we advocate. I shall bring him that bill this week, perhaps tomorrow, if possible. The minister promised me he would give it serious consideration. Then, if that legislation can be implemented in Canada, and I am sure it can, the minister could not say that we have nothing to suggest to solve the problem and to prevent wholesale dealers from taking undue advantage of the tax cut at the manufacturers' level. For all these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I deeply regret the government's decision to avail itself of the provisions of Standing Order 75C to end the debate and prevent hon. members from trying to convince the Minister of Finance to find a formula more flexible and respectful of the jurisdiction of the provinces and more specifically of the province of Quebec.
No matter what the minister may say, Mr. Speaker, the other finance ministers are in agreement, but this is not the first time it has been said in Canada that Quebec is not a province like the others. Quebec is the only French-speaking province in Canada and as such it is different from the other provinces. But it does not seek preferential treatment: from the economic point of view it wants to be treated by the central government just like all the other provinces. There is no doubt that the proposal the Minister of Finance has made is unacceptable because it flies in the face of the constitution; I therefore oppose this use of closure and we shall vote against this motion.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barney Danson (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what I find disturbing about what I hear today is that we are forgetting the essence of the debate, and what the debate is all about, namely, the economy of our country. Our economy needs that boost, support, and confidence being offered by the imaginative and innovative budget, together with a co-operative approach that has never taken place before in the history of our country. This has been on the part of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) who has consulted with the provinces.
It is not an easy or simple thing to talk with ten premiers or ministers of finance and obtain unanimity. They all realize they are big boys. They know what is at stake and that it is important the economy move forward with some cohesion, and that is exactly what the Minister of Finance was endeavouring to achieve, and to a large extent has achieved, except in one case.
That one case did not really involve the economy or the matter of cohesion. Indeed, it involved something almost in the reverse; stalling, delaying, not giving answers, and not proceeding, not because there was fundamental disagreement or an unwillingness to co-operate, and I realize that everyone cannot think precisely in the same way, but rather because those involved took the opportunity to help build their policy in order to demonstrate that they could only work within a framework

of sovereign association-a status that is quite different and does not depend on co-operation, courage, and innovation, such as shown by the Minister of Finance. That is something my friends opposite fail to understand.
We have here in the proposals of my colleague the makings of a way to maintain the momentum that is being built up in the economy. We have also the makings of the faith Canadians and people outside our country need, but which has been so badly shattered by the financial critic of the official opposition, in particular, and others from the other side. They have created a lack of confidence that has resulted in the lack of stability of our dollar. It has now returned to a reasonable state of stability, where it belongs. This is what has to be nurtured and preserved.
There are elements in the budget that will assist in providing impetus and the courage to exploit opportunities by the small business community across our country, a community which is so vital to our existence. The budget includes opportunities for research and development. The 150 per cent write off is not only a tax concession in itself for needed research and development, but is as well a signal to the businessmen and women of this country that this government has faith in them and in their ability to be innovative, and intends to back them up. It is an indication that this government wants them to be imaginative and get on with the job. This is followed of course by other announcements by the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Buchanan), which give further indications in that regard.
The important thing, Mr. Speaker, is to get on with the job-not to haggle amongst ourselves in what is a fragile world economy and one in which we have to compete desperately-to get on to other bills proposed by the Minister of Finance. For example, there is the provision for the write-off against future income of investment in small business, an extremely important element that I hope even the opposition can grasp. It is that which is called glove money in some cases, but I call it confidence money. It is money that brothers, parents, friends put up to invest in an entrepreneur's business, but cannot do so in many cases because it is hard earned money from people with small estates. This will at least give them the hope that if they are not successful they can write it off against future income. I mention that, not to take it out of context in this debate, but to put it in context, because these are all interrelated.
The monkey wrench is being thrown in not for reasons that the budget has been brought in and these new measures have been brought in, but for measures quite irrelevant to that, to demonstrate that provinces cannot co-operate with the federal government and with other provinces for the good of the entire country. That I find sad, and I think most people in the province of Quebec would find it sad too.
It is important, Mr. Speaker, that this bill be supported and that we get on with the business of the budget, that we move on to those other areas that need our attention, and that we
June 6, 1978

deal very realistically with the issues that are at stake here, which are whether we can work in co-operation and harmony in controlling the economy of this country, particularly at a time when it needs every bit of co-operation and support it can get. It is important that we allocate our time sensibly, get on with the job, and run the economy as it should be run, to the best of our ability with the greatest spirit we have.
Oh, oh!

I appreciate that perhaps the hon. members opposite do not understand, but the fact is that they are helping to destroy the confidence that we on this side of the House have in the people of this country, in the businessmen and women of this country, and in the potential of this country, which is very great indeed.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Miss Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the minister said as he began his remarks that what this debate was all about was the economy. Well, I would say to the minister that what this debate is about is the incompetence of this government, the incompetence of this government in the way in which it has handled the economy, the incompetence of this government in the way in which it approaches federal-provincial relations, the incompetence of this government in the way in which it runs the business of this parliament. That is what this debate is all about.
Hear, hear!

It is with a great deal of concern that I rise to speak on this motion today. I expressed my concern earlier in the debate when the bill was before the House, but I am doubly concerned today that we have a very unpopular bill, a tremendously unpopular bill that is about to be railroaded through the House by the motion of closure which we have before us.
What we have to remember, Mr. Speaker, is that closure is the ultimate weapon in parliament, a weapon to be brought in only in extreme situations. We have to ask ourselves is this such a situation? We have seen bills debated here for four, five six weeks, even months without closure being introduced. This is a bill which has been debated for a mere 25 hours, and now the government is imposing closure, imposing closure on a budget bill, a money bill, a bill dealing with the spending plans of the government. As such, it it a very important bill, one that it is the duty and role of parliament to examine and study extremely carefully.
It is the duty of the opposition, of those on this side of the House, to question how the government spends its money, and that is what we have been doing over these past days- questioning the government, asking for explanations, looking at the various measures in this bill. I might add we have been getting very little in the way of explanation from the government when we have raised these questions and doubts.
S.O.	75C
We have questioned in particular the one ludicrous measure in this bill that has received unanimous rejection from coast to coast, not only rejection by all members in the opposition parties in this parliament, but by people right across the country. It is clause 30 which has caused the government so much embarrassment, a measure designed to give direct tax rebates to the taxpayers of Quebec. That measure is the reason behind this closure motion being brought before us today. The government is invoking closure in order to get that embarrassing measure out of the way, and hopefully, so it thinks, out of the minds of the people, and out of the daily press where it is a continuing reminder, day after day, of the government's ineptitude and its lack of ability to handle the economy of the country.
This tax rebate which was conceived to replace a program that the government was unable to coerce the government of Quebec into accepting is an inept and clumsy solution to a problem that never should have arisen. It would never have arisen if the government truly understood the workings of the federal system. What the government has done in this debate and through this measure is to show that it fails to understand how a federal system should really work. As a result, what we have is closure, trying to sweep this ill-conceived measure under the rug.
This direct income tax rebate scheme is not only ill-conceived, it is modelled on an idea that is outdated and was outdated when it was first mentioned some ten years ago by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) but laid to rest at the Victoria conference and not resurrected since, until the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) put their heads together and brought about this disaster.
As I pointed out when I spoke on this matter earlier, the question of direct tax rebates to taxpayers in lieu of provincial participation in a federal-provincial agreement was raised during the period of the constitutional review between 1966 and 1971. The problem centred on what to do when a province did not want to join a federally initiated scheme upon which most of the other provinces had formally and officially agreed. At that time the Trudeau government proposed making payments directly to individuals. That proposal was attacked by every province in this country, including those which are strong supporters of a vigorous central government. It was seen to be completely unworkable and was unanimously rejected and, what is more, it was also rejected unanimously by the joint parliamentary committee on the constitution in 1972.
The Prime Minister accepted the overwhelming rejection that his proposal met with at that time, and he never tried to use it as a mechanism in federal-provincial programs. What I ask, sir, is what has changed now to cause this unwieldy proposal to be dusted off and put to the test at such a delicate time in our country's history, at a time when sensitivity is the most required ingredient in federal-provincial relations? Why did the Prime Minister think that he could do now, without consultation, what he could not do ten years ago, with consultation? I am at a loss to answer this, Mr. Speaker. I do know, and I want to repeat what a former premier of British

Columbia, Mr. Bennett, said ten years ago about this proposal. They were prophetic words indeed. He said, "If you introduce such a proposal you are going to play provincial governments against the federal government and you are going to break up this country and not build up Canadian unity. You are going to make for disunity."
The seeds of disunity have been implanted and nurtured by the government's intrasigent policy of proceeding with a method, such as it is doing, which was rejected ten years ago by all provinces and which has been rejected now by all parties in the National Assembly in the province of Quebec, and indeed by all outlets of opinion in the province of Quebec. This is a method which seems designed by this government to push the province of Quebec further into isolation.
Not content to introduce this divisive measure, the government is compounding the matter by ramming it home through the mechanism of closure. It has thus, in one move, dealt a double blow. It has attacked the roots of parliament and it has attacked the roots of our federal system. In this way it is demeaning the rights of individual members of parliament, and it is demeaning the rights of the provinces. Not even this government, with its penchant for stepping on both parliament and the provinces, has pushed its arrogance so far before. Today is surely a watershed in the arrogant life of a tyrannical government.
I say to members on the government side of the House that they should realize that in voting in favour of this motion of closure they are voting not only against the basic tenets of our federal system, but they are voting against the total membership of the National Assembly of the province of Quebec, and indeed they are voting against the overwhelming wishes of the people of the province of Quebec.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Bernard Loiselle (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate as I support without any reservation that motion for closure, and I believe it is essential to place it in its proper background and recall the reasons why the government chose that course of action. Although I may not be as close to the Parti Quebecois as the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle), my past experience makes me very close to provincial Liberals and I shall explain to the hon. member for Joliette why they had to take that position. But first, Mr. Speaker, I wish to explain why we chose that course of action.
Last January and February, when the provincial premiers and the federal government met at their conference, several of my friends, officials of the Quebec government with whom I discussed, everybody agreed about the problem we had to face and, considering the uncertainty caused by the high unemployment level, we had to encourage consumer spending to facilitate our economic recovery. Of course the government had

several means at its disposal. One of them was tried in January and February, that is a personal income tax reduction. Then there was the federal tax cut advocated by the Social Credit member for whom I have much respect. But the main beneficiaries of that measure would have been manufacturers and retailers rather than consumers. Yet all experts, including economists who are among the most ardent supporters of the Parti Quebecois, told to the provincial ministers and the federal minister that, considering our objective, the best means at our disposal was a sales tax cut. That stand required a lot of guts and a sense of innovation on the part of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), considering the determination of the Parti Quebecois to demonstrate that federalism cannot work.
The Minister of Finance had the guts to try that method. He consulted the ten provincial ministers. Obviously it was not easy, Mr. Speaker, and in our country where 75 per cent of manufactured goods are produced in Ontario and Quebec, where British Columbia's share is between 10 per cent and 13 per cent of the production particularly in the field of export plywood, there is consequently only 12 per cent left of the manufacturing production to be shared between seven other provinces and two territories. It then became unthinkable for the federal government to ask the provincial ministers to decide on a selective tax rebate. Where could Saskatchewan and Manitoba have effectively and efficiently applied such a selective measure?
The Ontario finance minister, Mr. Darcy McKeough, understood it and this is the reason why he accepted a tax rebate across the line. It is clear that with a selective measure, the two provinces which would have benefited most would be first Ontario and then Quebec. Yet the Ontario finance minister agreed to participate in a national scheme in order to serve the national interests. Those of our colleagues who are now talking about the constitution in this debate, I have to call them "constitutionalists." These are people who are playing some kind of a minuet without exactly knowing the tune to which they are dancing. In view of the fact that with the counter-proposal from the Canadian Minister of Finance, Quebec had the opportunity of spending that 1 percentage point which they were asked to inject, and spend precisely in those sectors which they chose, namely these four soft sectors.
As for the Quebec consumer, if we take for instance a family of 4 persons with a $10,000 income, we realize that with an overall reduction of 3 percentage points, and I am now adressing my remarks to the Progressive Conservative members who are changing their views just about every day, such a reduction of 3 percentage points on all items would increase the purchasing power of low-income people for more than a tax reduction applied only to four sectors. So, Mr. Speaker, the finance minister chose that method because, it is socially more equitable and economically more consistent with the over-all interests of the country. Mr. Parizeau has refused with his usual open-mindedness. Not only has he turned down our
June 6, 1978

proposals and decided not to negotiate for the past three weeks, not only has he refused to come to us with a counterproposal but he has played politics and applied a tax reduction of 8 percentage points on four sectors, Mr. Speaker and I am not convinced that the Quebec government is applying the right solution there.
Nobody, from Quebec in particular, has mentioned that since quotas were imposed on footwear and clothing we are having difficulty even supplying all retailers in British Columbia and Alberta, and I would like the Leader of the Opposition when he is in British Columbia and in his own province of Alberts, to tell the people, the retailers there who are making things tough for us in Ottawa, I would like him to tell them that he approves and encourages the decision made by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce under Mr. Jean Chretien, to cut imports.
Mr. Speaker, the most important thing at this time in these four sectors-they have orders-is for the government of Quebec, if it is looking for effective action, to make available to them a little more risk capital. The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce has set a program whereby we finance, not only in Quebec but across the country, 90 per cent of the studies made by those industries with a view to analyse the problem in a given company. Following that grants and loans of up to $1.5 million will help the industry to make a recovery. Unfortunately some companies are still going bankrupt not for lack of orders but because they produce at a loss, for instance instead of selling a pair of pants with a $1 profit, they lose 50 cents. What is required is not necessarily more orders, but the rationalization of their means of production. Mr. Speaker, if, instead of playing partisan politics, members of the opposition wanted to fully discuss the problem of those four sectors, they should come to me and I will give them a few pointers which will help them to speak more intelligently in Quebec.
Here is another thing. Mr. Speaker, when we took on that economic problem of getting the economy going again I would remind members of the opposition who want to bring the constitution into the debate that they all agree up to now that the federal government should be the one mainly responsible for the economy in this country. Now, in spite of the extensive decentralization advocated by the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) who does not know what he would decentralize, the fact is that the federal government collects only 40 per cent of taxes in this country, while 60 per cent are collected by provincial and municipal governments. Now, and here I shall follow the line of thought of the hon. member, if our government really wants to act in a responsible and effective way in a field where everybody agrees it should act, that is in the economic field, the hon. member should admit that with 40 per cent of taxes, he cannot speak of decentralization because with a little less money, the government will become inoperative to such an extent that it will no longer be able to play its role. I would understand then that he became a separatist, because it

is better to cut out the dead wood and take a new approach. Mr. Speaker, we have compared apples with oranges in this debate. Obviously, the hon. member for Joliette enjoyed flirting with the Parti Quebecois. He did not need the sales tax to do that; he had started long before. When the hon. member for Joliette who, after all, is still a Quebecker and the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) tell the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) that he should back down, I believe that the hon. member for Joliette should consider all the options that could be valid and truly helpful for Quebeckers instead of coming up with a new solution every day after reading the editorials in the morning newspapers.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to explain the position of the provincial Liberal party and of Mr. Ryan. Mr. Garneau, who was the economic adviser of the Liberal party up to the leadership convention, decided to support the federal government, and his new leader did not really examine Mr. Chretien's counter proposal in which he asked that the federal reduction of 2 per cent be applied on all the products, after which the province would be allowed to apply its 1 per cent reduction in whatever area it wished, and unfortunately, he did not have time to consider the proposal made during the weekend on the Thursday before the leadership convention and he took the position that I would have taken myself if I had been in his place. However, Mr. Speaker, he took this position on the advice of the Liberal member for Bonaventure, Mr. Levesque, who explained to him that when the Union Nationale, other good friends of the hon. member for Joliette, was in power and the Liberals made up the opposition in Quebec, on four different occasions, the provincial Liberals supported the federal Liberals, and after consultations, dialogues and negotiations between the Union Nationale and the government in Ottawa, the provincial Liberals looked as though they had adopted a holier-than-thou attitude and had been more federalist than the federalists in Ottawa.
Mr. Levesque, and I want to explain this to Mr. La Salle who is a good politician, Mr. Levesque explained to Mr. Ryan that it would be very dangerous to support openly the federal Liberals in case there was some sort of compromise which would give Quebeckers the impression that if the Liberals had been in power in Quebec rather than the Independentists, Quebec's share would have been less. However, Mr. Speaker, and the hon. member for Joliette should certainly recognize this, it remains that Mr. Ryan has effectively suggested a formula that the Minister of Finance accepted last week, whether or not it is a rebate, and the Leader of the Opposition is shaking his head in disagreement. That is why the government wants to implement this proposal this year rather than next year. The Leader of the Opposition says that those $85 cheques will not help the poor, but next year about 100,000 fewer would be helped. But the Leader of the Opposition will certainly understand that the Liberal government, always the champion of the underprivileged in this country, had to-

Mr. Speaker, I hope that the new Liberal leader in Quebec will not read the words of the hon. member for Chambly (Mr. Loiselle), because judging from what he said, you would think that Mr. Ryan is stupid rather than intelligent. Apparently, he had not understood the minister's proposal correctly, that is, Mr. Levesque had apparently misled him and finally-No, frankly I think Mr. Ryan is more intelligent than that and I intend to trust Mr. Ryan more than the hon. member for Chambly who just tried to teach us a lesson at his government's prompting. Like all the others in front of me, he toes the party line.
I repeat today that because of this guillotine imposed by the government, this is a very sad day for the members of this House and particularly for the members from Quebec, Mr. Speaker.
Mr. Speaker, I certainly do not believe in the arguments put forward by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) and the hon. member for Chambly in his malicious comments, saying that we are yet more hon. members who want to please the Quebec separatists, refusing to recognize that the Minister of Finance faces a unanimous National Assembly and a unanimous official opposition proposals. Would it be then that the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister alone hold the truth in the matter?
Mr. Speaker, I think we have proof here of disconcerting and unbelievable treason with regard to the fundamental question. I trust, Mr. Speaker, that the ten minutes allotted us will enable the hon. members of this House to reject this motion for closure, motion that is odious in a parliament such as ours, and on a debate that deserves some continuity.
The Minister of Finance has the gall to move a motion of closure, knowing full well that there is still unanimity in Quebec, at this very moment, and when he tries to make out a solution is forthcoming within hours, and asks us to support this motion of closure, on a bill which is inacceptable in principle, even less so for Quebeckers, I say, it takes nerve.
I also wonder how it is that the 60 Quebec members opposite are hiding behind the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). I am well aware of the fact that they are usually elected on the Prime Minister's coattails. I think that in view of the present situation, they are panic-striken and are more worried than they care to admit. It would be timely to repeat what so many Quebeckers asked me over the weekend: "Where are those valiant Quebec MPs who are supposed to defend our rights in Ottawa? Let those gallant Liberals who had pledged to carry
[Mr. Loiselle (Chambly).l
out the Prime Minister's promise of a just society stand up and be counted."
And what about the hope generated by the arrival of those three doves at the House of Commons, two of whom have already left for more secure havens and the third, according to the last Gallup poll, is in a bad way but would rather put up with anything than quit. Mr. Speaker, we know that the Minister of Finance had to make concessions in view of his colossal blunder, his clumsy negotiations and attitude. Of course, the government will boast of their flexibility, which they have not shown any sign of over the last ten years, and all of a sudden, on realizing they have painted themselves into a corner they will claim to be open-minded. We have been pressing the Minister of Finance, for the past two months, to consider and reply to Quebec's proposal.
Can anyone in this House argue that the Quebec government's proposal on behalf of those sectors where problems are the most acute was a bad one? As I said before, for the sake of the so-called unanimity in the National Assembly, they will keep manipulating people with comments of all kinds, such as the ones the hon. member for Chambly (Mr. Loiselle) made earlier. I do not want to give him more importance than he has. This debate started two months ago and 1 think it is the first time I have heard him say anything on this matter. Obviously, he has been well briefed and instructed by members of his party. Perhaps the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Tessier) will make a few comments presently. I hope he does. I heard him say that this proposal of the Minister of Finance was a political catastrophy. The next day he almost clapped his desk to pieces after the Minister of Finance defended his stand. That worries me a little, but this afternoon he has another chance to shape up and I trust he will. Other members on the other side have also expressed their disapproval and they are absent today. I suppose they have other responsibilities.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance referred to flexibility in connection with our unyielding and fierce position for the past two months, but he had to change his mind and alter his proposal, and thanks to us on this side of the House, the Quebec finance minister and the provinces will not be hoodwinked and forced to accept the dictatorial measures of the federal government. Today he speaks about flexibility, but it only proves his weakness and his ridiculous incompetence from which he is absolved by the Prime Minister each time he answers a question we put to him. I never thought the Prime Minister would go that far.
As a responsible head of state, we have been asking him for the past two weeks to take up the matter personally, since his Minister of Finance has shown his incompetence. Well aware that the Minister of Finance could no longer negotiate with his Quebec counterpart, the Prime Minister has declined to assume his responsibilities and call a meeting with the Quebec premier. He has not done so but encouraged his Minister of Finance in his colossal error; now they are telling us that no

special arrangements are to be made whereas we know perfectly well that on the initial proposal there have been some arrangements with certain provinces. But in the case of Quebec, arrangements are alleged to divide the country and undermine federalism. This is the kind of comments some people conveniently forget. As soon as we opposed the bill, the Prime Minister charged all supporters of the Parizeau proposal with undermining federalism. The Minister of Finance stated that that proposal was likely to divide the country but when the provincial parties headed by Mr. Ryan and Mr. Biron and others and the unanimous opposition on this side and some other sectors of the economy joined the official opposition side, the Prime Minister did not dare repeat his charges in this House. He was less brave here than he was with the media at the time of his first press conference. The Minister of Finance also changed his attitude many times but he tried almost every week to make us believe that we just wanted to support a proposal by a government with very particular option.
Mr. Speaker, at no time have we supported the Quebec government for political reasons. We have supported what we felt were Quebec's interests, and we have fought for a basic principle whereby under a new federalism, the provinces should be allowed to discuss this issue freely and participate in a decision as important as the one proposed by the Minister of Finance. But these negotiations which are said-
That is exactly what they did-

I have just heard the hon. member for Laval (Mr. Roy) who will certainly vote for closure and put a gag on all members without hearing first about the forthcoming solution. Of course, we are all anxious to find such a solution, and a responsible government would certainly have dealt differently with hon. members who are as eager and willing to safeguard Quebec's interests. I suggest that we were entitled to expect a better performance than the one we have witnessed for the past two months.
I know full well, Mr. Speaker, that when the Prime Minister was facing an election call two weeks ago, the position of the Liberals influenced the decision he had to take in terms of an election call which was postponed to a later date, and I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the Quebeckers in this House will raise on this closure motion-

speakeroldname: Mr. Yvon Pinard (Parliamentary Secretary to President of Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the motion moved by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) is based on a Standing Order which was passed by this parliament precisely to avoid any

counter abuses. Under this standing order, a minister sponsoring a bill in the House can, by way of a motion, put an end to the debate at a given stage of the study of any bill when it is required by the interests of society and the state, when it seems obvious that the opposition parties are more interested in playing politics than in the subject matter of the bill at stake and that they ignore the well being of the collectivity. So the question arising out of this motion is whether or not the Minister of Finance is justified to resort to a rule which is part of the standing orders of the House of Commons of Canada to limit the debate on the second reading of a bill containing 59 clauses spread over 66 pages.
Now, what we have witnessed during the past ten days, when we were supposed to discuss the whole bill and when actually most interventions dealt only with clause 30 of the bill, is that about ten days have indeed been spent so far merely rising against and attempting to politicize a situation without even trying to suggest really concrete and useful proposals. In the course of that debate which has lasted for ten days now at the stage of second reading, I have never heard the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle), the hon. member for Brome-Mis-sisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) or other members of other opposition parties concerned with that issue come forward with some useful suggestion in an attempt to solve what was at the beginning a problem, a matter of principle which is now settled and might have become a simple matter of finding the best way to transfer the money. Not a single constructive suggestion has been made, only destructive and negative criticism.
I find that unacceptable and irresponsible, Mr. Speaker, from people who suggest they want the good of Canadian citizens. I can see that the opposition leader is trying to tell me something. I will be happy to give him a briefing after I finish my short statement, Mr. Speaker, in order to correctly explain to him the principles which are contained in Bill C-56 and which he apparently missed completely. Instead of trying to support the cause of the Parti Quebecois, Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition should endeavour to demonstrate that right from the start of this controversy there was evidence of pettiness on the part of one of the provincial ministers of Finance, that there was a lack of honest cooperation on the part of one of the provincial ministers of finance while the nine others, who were consulted by the federal Minister of Finance, agreed on a helpful solution for the Canadian economy.
They allowed the Canadian government to intervene in a field of provincial jurisdiction, namely sales taxes. They allowed the Minister of Finance to reimburse them the equivalent of two out of three points of general sales tax cut in Canada. However, the Quebec minister of finance dozed through the three weeks of negotiations. He sent his officials. He came. He took part in the discussions. He did not take a stand, that, from the start, it must be pointed out and can never be stressed enough, Mr. Speaker. That was unacceptable
June 6, 1978

meanness on the part of a provincial minister of finance, that can only be explained by the objectives pursued by the government of which this minister of finance is a member, that is, destroying our country and proving that federalism cannot work. I suggest it is irresponsible for a Leader of the Opposition of a Progressive Conservative member from Quebec to side with a Minister of Finance who resorted to such pettiness. Mr. Speaker, I hear the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle), yelling from behind the curtains, that I should accuse Mr. Ryan. All Mr. Ryan did was to support a motion dealing with principles. As I said, this goes to show that the hon. member for Joliette is not aware of all the facts, or he does not fully understand the situation.
